_meta.notes: Definitions and sanity checks for standard business metrics. Consult BEFORE defining a metric in an analysis, and state the definition you used. The ranges in 'sanity' are rough plausibility bands to catch calculation errors (a churn of 90% a month, a gross margin of 140%); they are not benchmarks to quote, and they vary by industry, size and stage. If the user's own definition differs, use theirs and say so. Lookup: python3 scripts/stats.py define NAME

churn_rate.name: Customer (logo) churn rate
churn_rate.formula: customers who left during the period / customers at the START of the period
churn_rate.denominator: customers active at the start of the period; new customers won during the period are NOT in the denominator
mistakes: Dividing by the average or the end count, or including customers who joined and left inside the period
Multiplying monthly churn by 12 for annual churn; use 1 - (1 - m)^12 instead
Comparing monthly and annual churn, or a new-customer cohort with the whole base
Counting paused, downgraded or failed-payment accounts as churned without saying so
churn_rate.sanity: Monthly: enterprise B2B under 1%, SMB software 1-5%, consumer subscriptions 4-10%. Above 15% a month means either a trial-heavy product or a calculation error.

revenue_churn.name: Gross revenue churn
revenue_churn.formula: (recurring revenue lost to cancellations + downgrades in the period) / recurring revenue at the START of the period
revenue_churn.denominator: recurring revenue at the start of the period
mistakes: Netting expansion against losses; that is net revenue retention, not churn
Including one-off or usage revenue that was never recurring
Mixing currencies or annual contracts not converted to a monthly amount
revenue_churn.sanity: Between 0% and 100% by definition. Above 100% is impossible; a monthly value above 10% for a mature product deserves a second look.

retention_rate.name: Customer retention rate
retention_rate.formula: (customers at end of period - new customers acquired in the period) / customers at start of period
retention_rate.denominator: customers at the start of the period
mistakes: Leaving new customers in the numerator, which can push retention above 100%
Reporting it as 1 - churn without checking both used the same start-of-period base
Quoting a period-end snapshot as if it were a cohort curve
retention_rate.sanity: 0-100%. Annual B2B logo retention is commonly 80-95%; below 50% a year is a serious problem or a consumer product.

cohort_retention.name: Cohort retention curve (day N or month N)
cohort_retention.formula: users from a signup cohort who were active in period N / users in that cohort
cohort_retention.denominator: the cohort size at signup (fixed for every N)
mistakes: Defining 'active' differently across periods, or counting any login as retained when the product needs a key action
Averaging cohorts of very different sizes without weighting
Reading incomplete recent cohorts (not yet N days old) as poor retention
Using rolling 'active in day N or later' (unbounded) for some cohorts and exact-day for others
cohort_retention.sanity: Should fall or flatten, never rise sharply. Consumer apps: day 1 about 20-40%, day 30 about 3-10%. B2B: month 12 logo retention 80-95%.

nrr.name: Net revenue retention
nrr.formula: (starting recurring revenue + expansion - contraction - churn) from the SAME customers / starting recurring revenue
nrr.denominator: recurring revenue at the start from the customers who existed then
mistakes: Including revenue from customers acquired after the start date
Mixing a monthly figure with the annual benchmark
Ignoring that a few large accounts can drive the whole number
nrr.sanity: Can exceed 100%. Typical software 90-115%; above 130% is exceptional; above 200% is usually a tiny base or an error.

grr.name: Gross revenue retention
grr.formula: (starting recurring revenue - contraction - churn) from the same customers / starting recurring revenue
mistakes: Letting expansion revenue in (then it is NRR)
Not capping each customer at their starting amount
grr.sanity: Cannot exceed 100%. Typical 80-95%; below 70% signals a leaky product.

cac.name: Customer acquisition cost
cac.formula: sales and marketing cost in the period / NEW customers acquired in the period
cac.denominator: new customers only (not total customers, not leads)
mistakes: Counting only ad spend and leaving out salaries, tools and agency fees (say which you used)
Mixing blended CAC (all new customers) with paid CAC (only ad-driven customers)
Ignoring the lag between spend and the sale for long sales cycles
Dividing by leads or trials instead of paying customers
cac.sanity: Compare with first-year gross profit per customer. CAC above the gross profit a customer brings in 12-18 months is a warning; consumer CAC of a few dollars to tens of dollars, enterprise CAC in the tens of thousands, are both normal.

ltv.name: Customer lifetime value
ltv.formula: average revenue per customer per period x gross margin % / churn rate per period
ltv.denominator: churn rate for the same period as the revenue figure (monthly with monthly)
mistakes: Using revenue instead of gross profit
Tiny churn producing an absurd lifetime of decades; cap the lifetime at 3-5 years
Using blended churn for a segment with very different churn
Treating a projection as an observed number; state that it is modelled
ltv.sanity: Implied lifetime = 1 / churn. A lifetime above 5 years needs evidence; LTV below CAC means the business loses money on each customer.

ltv_cac.name: LTV to CAC ratio
ltv_cac.formula: customer lifetime value / customer acquisition cost
mistakes: Using LTV built on revenue rather than gross profit
Comparing an LTV over 5 years to a CAC that ignores half the costs
Reading it without payback time: 3x that takes 6 years to earn back can still starve cash
ltv_cac.sanity: Around 3x is a common target. Below 1x loses money; above 5x may mean under-investing in growth, or an inflated LTV.

cac_payback.name: CAC payback period
cac_payback.formula: CAC / (average monthly revenue per customer x gross margin %)
mistakes: Using revenue rather than gross profit
Using annual revenue with monthly CAC or the reverse
Ignoring churn during the payback window
cac_payback.sanity: SMB software 6-18 months; enterprise 18-30 months. Under 3 months is rare and worth double-checking; over 36 months is dangerous.

arpu.name: Average revenue per user (or account)
arpu.formula: revenue in the period / average number of ACTIVE users (or accounts) in the period
arpu.denominator: active users on the same basis as the revenue (paying only for ARPPU)
mistakes: Including free users without saying so; ARPPU divides by paying users only
Using end-of-period users when the base grew fast
Mixing one-off and recurring revenue
arpu.sanity: Should sit near your price points. An ARPU above your highest plan means multi-seat accounts or an error.

mrr_arr.name: Monthly and annual recurring revenue
mrr_arr.formula: MRR = sum of monthly-normalised subscription fees of active customers; ARR = 12 x MRR
mistakes: Including one-off fees, services, or usage spikes in ARR
Counting a signed contract that has not started, or one that has ended
Annualising a single strong month of non-recurring revenue
Not normalising annual or quarterly plans to months
mrr_arr.sanity: ARR should be within a few percent of 12 x the latest MRR. Month-to-month MRR jumps above 30% need a named cause.

conversion_rate.name: Conversion rate
conversion_rate.formula: conversions / visitors (or sessions, or leads: name the denominator)
conversion_rate.denominator: the unit that could have converted, on the same time window as the conversions
mistakes: Mixing users in the numerator with sessions in the denominator
Counting a repeat visitor as a new chance to convert without saying so
Comparing conversion rates whose traffic mix differs; check rate versus mix (drivers.py --ratio)
Averaging daily rates instead of dividing total conversions by total visitors
conversion_rate.sanity: E-commerce site-wide 1-4%; landing pages 2-10%; paid social on cold traffic under 2%. Above 20% is only plausible for high-intent flows (a checkout, a demo request from a customer).

funnel_conversion.name: Funnel step and overall conversion
funnel_conversion.formula: step conversion = users reaching step n / users reaching step n-1; overall = users reaching the last step / users at the first step
funnel_conversion.denominator: the previous step, on the same cohort of users
mistakes: Counting events instead of distinct users at each step
Different time windows per step, so late converters are missing at the bottom
Steps that can be skipped, so a later step exceeds an earlier one
Multiplying rates from different cohorts
funnel_conversion.sanity: Counts must not increase down the funnel for a strict funnel. Overall conversion is the product of the step rates; check that it matches.

aov.name: Average order value
mistakes: Dividing by customers or sessions (that is a different metric)
Letting a few very large orders drive the mean; look at the median as well
Mixing gross and net of refunds or discounts between periods
aov.sanity: Near the range of your prices times a typical basket. If AOV moves, split it into price, units per order and mix (drivers.py --ratio revenue,count).

gross_margin.name: Gross margin
mistakes: Dividing by cost (that is markup)
Leaving out shipping, payment fees or hosting that belong in cost of goods
Using operating costs (rent, marketing) as if they were cost of goods
gross_margin.sanity: Cannot exceed 100%. Software 70-90%, retail 25-50%, services 30-60%, marketplaces (net revenue) 60-90%. Negative means selling below cost.

margin_vs_markup.name: Margin versus markup
margin_vs_markup.formula: margin = (price - cost) / price; markup = (price - cost) / cost; margin = markup / (1 + markup); markup = margin / (1 - margin)
margin_vs_markup.denominator: price for margin, cost for markup
mistakes: Treating a 50% markup as a 50% margin; it is a 33.3% margin
Pricing at cost x (1 + target margin), which gives less margin than intended
margin_vs_markup.sanity: Markup is always larger than margin. A 100% markup is a 50% margin; a margin can never reach 100%.

cagr.name: Compound annual growth rate
cagr.denominator: starting value; years = time BETWEEN the first and last observation
mistakes: Using the number of data points as the number of years (5 yearly values span 4 years)
Using it when the start value is zero or negative
Reading it as a smooth path when the series is volatile or has a one-off peak at the end
Comparing CAGRs computed over different windows
cagr.sanity: Sustained CAGR above 100% is rare beyond small bases. Always show start, end and years next to it.

growth_vs_points.name: Percent growth versus percentage points
growth_vs_points.formula: growth % = (new - old) / old; for a rate, change in points = new rate - old rate
growth_vs_points.unit: percent, or percentage points for rates
mistakes: Saying a rate rose 50% when it went from 2% to 3% (that is +1 point, +50% relative; say which)
Averaging monthly growth rates arithmetically; use the compound rate
Starting from a tiny base, which makes any change look huge
A fall of 50% then a rise of 50% does not return to the start
growth_vs_points.sanity: Growth cannot go below -100%. Recompute from the two values before quoting it.

moving_average.name: Moving average
moving_average.formula: mean of the last N observations (trailing) or N centred on the point
mistakes: Choosing a window that hides the pattern; use 7 for daily data with weekday effects, 4 or 13 for weekly
Reporting the first N-1 points as if complete windows existed
Averaging rates without weighting by their denominators
Reading a trailing average as a forecast
moving_average.sanity: The smoothed series must lie within the range of the raw data and lag it. If it does not, the window or the alignment is wrong.

dau_mau.name: DAU/MAU stickiness
dau_mau.formula: average daily active users over a 30-day window / monthly active users for the same window
dau_mau.unit: ratio between 0 and 1 (often shown as percent)
mistakes: Dividing one day's DAU by a different month's MAU
Using different definitions of 'active' for the two counts
Counting logins from bots or background sync
dau_mau.sanity: Between 0 and 100%. Typical products 10-25%; social and messaging 40-60%; above 60% is exceptional. It can never exceed 100%.

nps.name: Net Promoter Score
nps.formula: % promoters (scores 9-10) - % detractors (scores 0-6); scores 7-8 count only in the total
mistakes: Averaging the 0-10 scores instead
Ignoring the response count and response bias (unhappy or delighted customers answer more)
Treating 7s and 8s as promoters
Comparing scores across industries
nps.sanity: Between -100 and +100. Often 0-50 in software; above 70 is rare. Under 100 responses the score moves by more than 10 points from noise.

roas.name: Return on ad spend
roas.formula: revenue attributed to ads / ad spend
mistakes: Ignoring margin: break-even ROAS is 1 / gross margin (a 40% margin needs 2.5x)
Attributing revenue to ads that would have happened anyway
Comparing platform-reported ROAS (self-attributed, often overlapping) with your own totals
roas.sanity: Break-even is above 1x. Platform ROAS 2-6x is common; above 15x usually means brand searchers or double counting.

roi.name: Return on investment
mistakes: Leaving out staff time, tools or opportunity cost
Ignoring how long the return took (10% in a month versus 10% in ten years)
Counting revenue as gain instead of profit
roi.sanity: Cannot go below -100%. ROI above 1000% deserves a check of the cost side.

ctr.name: Click-through rate
ctr.denominator: impressions or delivered messages, not sends that bounced
mistakes: Mixing unique and total clicks
Using opens as the denominator for email without saying so (click-to-open is a different metric)
Comparing across channels
ctr.sanity: Display ads 0.05-0.5%, paid search 2-6%, email 1-5% of delivered. Above 30% suggests bots or a counting error.

ad_unit_costs.name: CPM, CPC and CPA
ad_unit_costs.formula: CPM = cost / impressions x 1000; CPC = cost / clicks; CPA = cost / conversions; CPA = CPC / conversion rate
mistakes: Forgetting the x1000 in CPM
Comparing CPA across campaigns with different conversion definitions
Optimising CPC alone when the conversion rate falls
ad_unit_costs.sanity: The identity CPA = CPC / conversion rate must hold; if it does not, one of the three inputs is on a different basis.

repeat_purchase_rate.name: Repeat purchase rate
repeat_purchase_rate.formula: customers with 2 or more orders in the window / customers with at least 1 order in the window
repeat_purchase_rate.denominator: customers who bought at least once in the window
mistakes: Not stating the window; a longer window always gives a higher rate
Counting split shipments or one order with several lines as repeats
Judging recent customers who have not had time to repurchase
repeat_purchase_rate.sanity: Consumer e-commerce 15-40% over 12 months; consumables can be much higher. Above 80% needs a subscription explanation.

refund_rate.name: Refund or return rate
refund_rate.formula: refunded orders (or units, or amount) / orders (or units, or amount) sold in the same cohort
refund_rate.denominator: the same unit and the same sale cohort as the numerator
mistakes: Dividing refunds issued this month by sales this month (refunds lag the sale)
Mixing order count in one and revenue in the other
Reading the most recent months as low when refunds have not arrived yet
refund_rate.sanity: Software 1-5%, general e-commerce 5-15%, apparel 20-30% or more. Above 40% points to a product or a data problem.

inventory_turnover.name: Inventory turnover
inventory_turnover.formula: cost of goods sold / average inventory value; days of inventory = 365 / turnover
inventory_turnover.denominator: average inventory at cost over the period
mistakes: Using sales instead of cost of goods, or year-end inventory instead of the average
Ignoring seasonality when comparing a peak-season snapshot
inventory_turnover.sanity: Grocery 10-20 a year, apparel 3-6, furniture 2-4. Under 1 means slow stock or an error in the inventory value.

burn_runway.name: Burn rate and runway
burn_runway.formula: net burn = cash out - cash in per month; runway (months) = cash balance / net burn
burn_runway.denominator: current monthly net burn (use the recent 3-month average)
mistakes: Using gross burn (spending only) when revenue offsets it
Dividing by a best-month burn; use a recent average
Forgetting known future costs or that hiring raises burn
burn_runway.sanity: Runway under 6 months means fundraising or cutting now; over 24 months is comfortable. Net burn cannot be negative unless the company is cash positive.

quick_ratio.name: SaaS quick ratio
quick_ratio.formula: (new MRR + expansion MRR) / (churned MRR + contraction MRR)
quick_ratio.denominator: MRR lost in the same period
mistakes: Mixing periods for the numerator and denominator
Dividing by zero in a month with no losses; the ratio is then undefined
quick_ratio.sanity: Above 1 means growing. Around 4 is considered strong; under 1 means shrinking.

rule_of_40.name: Rule of 40
rule_of_40.formula: revenue growth % + profit margin % (state the margin: EBITDA, operating or free cash flow)
rule_of_40.denominator: not a ratio; a sum of two percentages
mistakes: Mixing a year-over-year growth with a quarterly margin
Switching the margin definition between years
rule_of_40.sanity: 40 or more is the usual bar. A value above 100 means a very small or unusual company.

win_rate.name: Sales win rate
win_rate.formula: deals won / (deals won + deals lost) among deals CLOSED in the period
win_rate.denominator: closed deals (won plus lost); open deals are excluded
win_rate.unit: percent by count or by value (say which)
mistakes: Counting open deals as losses
Mixing deals created in the period with deals closed in it
Ignoring deals that went silent and were never marked lost
win_rate.sanity: B2B 15-30% is typical; 5% for cold outbound; above 60% suggests deals are qualified too late or losses are not recorded.

pipeline_coverage.name: Pipeline coverage
pipeline_coverage.formula: open pipeline value for the period / remaining quota (or target) for the period
mistakes: Counting the whole pipeline regardless of expected close date
Using coverage without the historical win rate; 3x only works with a win rate near 33%
pipeline_coverage.sanity: Roughly 1 / win rate is needed: about 3-4x for a 25-33% win rate. Below 2x is thin.

average_of_rates.name: Averaging rates and averages
average_of_rates.formula: combined rate = total numerators / total denominators (not the mean of the group rates)
average_of_rates.denominator: the summed denominators of all groups
mistakes: Averaging percentages from groups of different size (a 50% of 10 and a 10% of 1000 is about 10.4%, not 30%)
Averaging daily averages instead of total / total
Simpson's paradox: a rate can rise in every segment and fall overall when the mix shifts; use drivers.py --ratio to separate rate from mix
average_of_rates.sanity: The combined rate always lies between the smallest and largest group rate and sits closer to the big groups.

active_users.name: Active users (DAU, WAU, MAU)
active_users.formula: distinct users who performed a qualifying action in the window
active_users.denominator: not a ratio; state the action and the window
mistakes: Counting events or sessions instead of distinct users
Letting 'active' mean any page view for one number and a key action for another
Counting the same person twice across devices, or bots
Comparing calendar-month MAU with a rolling 30-day MAU
active_users.sanity: DAU <= WAU <= MAU always. MAU larger than the total registered users means anonymous visitors are included.

median_vs_mean.name: Median versus mean
median_vs_mean.formula: mean = sum / count; median = the middle value once sorted
mistakes: Reporting the mean of skewed data (revenue per customer, time to resolve, order value) as 'typical'
Averaging in zeros or blanks by accident
Comparing a mean to a median
median_vs_mean.sanity: If the mean is more than 20% away from the median, the data are skewed: report the median, or both, and say why.

yoy_seasonality.name: Year-over-year versus month-over-month
yoy_seasonality.formula: YoY = this period / same period last year - 1; MoM = this period / previous period - 1
mistakes: Calling a seasonal December-to-January fall a decline; compare with the same month last year
Comparing periods of different length (28 vs 31 days, or different weekday counts)
Comparing a partial current month with a full previous month
Ignoring one-off events (a promotion, a holiday shift) in the base period
yoy_seasonality.sanity: If MoM swings repeat the same way every year, the pattern is seasonal. Check at least two full years before calling anything a trend.
